picks.excerpt: Harriman House claims a trade publishing first with The Everything Code by macro analyst Raoul Pal, produced with a proprietary AI tool trained exclusively on the author's own existing work. It is a concrete template for 'AI-facilitated' authorship — a model trained on one author's corpus, disclosed on the jacket — rather than an anonymous LLM draft.
picks.rationale: First named trade-publishing model for AI-facilitated authorship — a corpus-of-one tool plus jacket disclosure gives editors and authors an actual template to copy tomorrow.

picks.excerpt: Originality.ai scanned 2,034 paperback religion books on Amazon and found 63% were likely AI-written — 78% in witchcraft, 76% Hinduism, 74% Taoism, versus 22% in Satanism. Likely-AI titles averaged $16.84 and 170 pages against $18.96 and 208 pages for human-written ones, a measurable shape for the AI slop flooding a single retail category.
picks.rationale: Puts hard numbers — category, price and page-count signatures — on AI slop in one retail vertical, turning a vague complaint into a measurable market pattern.

picks.excerpt: A US class action filed by textbook authors alleges OpenAI ingested hundreds of academic volumes. The suit argues that if LLMs keep ingesting new editions as they appear, instructors may drop textbook adoptions entirely in favour of AI 'substitutes' — putting the economics of educational authorship, not just the training question, on trial.
picks.rationale: New class action that moves the training fight past copying and onto substitution — whether AI replaces textbook adoption itself, which reframes risk for every educational publisher.

picks.excerpt: Stacey Anderson explains why Codex-style agents aren't smarter models — they just have access to your files — and shows a low-stress way for authors to give an AI direct access to a manuscript project folder instead of pasting chapters into a chat box.
picks.rationale: Most directly actionable item in the pool: a concrete shift from copy-paste chat to file-access agents that a writer can set up on their own manuscript folder today.

picks.excerpt: A pointed essay against the 'AI reading buddy' — the chat-with-your-book, summarise-this-chapter layer now being bolted onto ereaders and reading apps. The argument: bulletpointising books optimises away the difficulty that reading is actually for, and product teams shipping reading assistants are designing the wrong metric.
picks.rationale: The reader-side counterweight to the week's production news, and a direct critique of the AI reading-assistant features product teams are currently shipping into ereaders.
